sources.title: UNESCO: Pergamon and its Multi-Layered Cultural Landscape
sources.note: Official World Heritage statement read directly. Hellenistic capital, hillside planning, library and gymnasium; subsequent Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman settlement. Avoids the imprecise short-description claim that the city was founded in the third century BCE.

sources.title: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin: Pergamon exhibition wall texts, 2018
sources.note: Direct PDF, pages 3 to 4 dynasty; page 5 altar; pages 8 to 9 palace mosaics. All sections treated as one work. The modern panorama represents 129 CE and is not used as an Attalid-era eyewitness.

sources.title: Noah Kaye: The Attalids of Pergamon and Anatolia, 2023
sources.note: Original open-access research. Introduction political history and chapter 5 Hastening to the Gymnasium read directly and through indexed original text. One combined work budget covers all chapters: no artificial chapter-level expansion. 188 settlement follows the earlier battle of Magnesia; avoid the introduction shorthand that appears to put that battle in 188.

sources.title: Monika Trümper: Bathing Culture in Hellenistic Domestic Architecture
sources.note: Original scholarly paper read directly, printed pages 531 and 545. Survey counts 39 known Pergamon dwellings: 18 courtyard and 21 peristyle houses, including palaces, most built third to first centuries BCE. No Hellenistic bathroom identified in this sample; late-first-century BCE additions belong to later Roman phase. Findings are explicitly attributed to this survey, not presented as all houses ever found.

sources.title: Anneke Keweloh-Kaletta: Keramik in Pergamon durch die Lupe betrachtet
sources.note: DAI primary pottery-research abstract, direct and indexed German original. Published 26 May 2026 in issue 2025. Regional clay goods dominate Hellenistic and Imperial assemblages; imports from Italy also present. Only the broad dated ceramic observation and analytical method are used, no unsupported individual recipe or Hellenistic Italian-import date.

sources.title: Berslan Korkut: New Insights and Questions on the Water Supply System of the Ancient City of Pergamon, 2022
sources.note: DAI primary field-research report read directly/indexed. Madradag pipeline dated 180 to 160 BCE; 42 km and about 200,000 pipe sections are Garbrecht estimates, not a modern full count. Newly observed aqueduct attribution remains probable. Stamps and differing clay fabrics complicate assignments to separate pipelines.

sources.title: National Technical University of Athens, ITIA: Pergamon cistern
sources.note: Institutional hydraulic inventory. Full indexed original gives dimensions and fire-reservoir interpretation after H. Fahlbusch 2012; direct text omits descriptive body. Human bucket chains are a reconstruction, not an ancient testimony. Public text explicitly labels interpretation.

sources.title: Christina Williamson and Alexandra Katevaini: Deep-mapping the Asklepieion of Pergamon
sources.note: University of Groningen research project, indexed original read in full relevant phases; dynamic direct page exposes no body. Phase 2 incubation area circa 275 to 240 BCE, phase 3 early-second-century BCE enclosure and sacred road. Later Roman buildings and Aristides testimony are not projected backward.

sources.title: J. Thomas: Art and natural science in the Hellenistic world, Oxford DPhil, 2016
sources.note: Indexed original Volume I printed page 213 and Volume II figure 181 caption, printed page 93, independently provide exact uppercase Greek and translation. Direct ORA PDF fetch failed; not a personal visual reading of ancient tesserae. Object and translation independently corroborated by museum foundation 2025. No use of the paragraph’s ancient parchment-invention story as fact.

sources.title: Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz: Pergamonmuseum architecture under construction, 11 February 2025
sources.note: Museum foundation direct text, paragraphs on Hephaistion mosaic and Athena Parthenos. Confirms translation, palace provenance, illusionistic loose corner; library statue of Athena second century BCE and relation to Athenian model. Modern installation is not ancient altar-floor placement.

sources.title: ASCSA, Hesperia: Earliest Athenian New Style Bronze Coins, Stoa of Attalos discussion
sources.note: Indexed original scholarly text, printed page 313, verifies Attalos II gift, reign 159 to 138 BCE, two storeys, 21 shops per level and colonnades. Architecture used as evidence of royal patronage abroad, not Pergamon city layout.

sources.title: Alessandro Viscogliosi: From Pergamon to Rome and from Rome to Pergamon, in Art of the Hellenistic Kingdoms, Metropolitan Museum
sources.note: Original scholarly museum volume read directly, PDF pages 94 to 96 (zero-based 93 to 95). Bequest, Aristonikos rebellion, Roman province after 129 BCE; Pergamon not sacked and civic privileges retained under Roman supremacy. All contributions in volume treated as one source work.

sources.title: Human History Map: imported Pergamon geometry
sources.note: Local decoded single feature, -200 to -100, bounds 26.062 to 27.999 E and 38.956 to 40.451 N. Restricted western-Anatolian outline, not an accurate maximum Attalid empire. Exact record membership and lack of runtime card/override checked; no other Attalid aliases found.

proposedOverrides.name: Pergamon
proposedOverrides.summary: Attalid capital known for hillside architecture, scholarship, art and water engineering.

batchIdentityNotes.association: One exact indexed record; no new alias.
batchIdentityNotes.scope: Capital and Attalid kingdom, with early Roman transition. The imported polygon is restricted relative to post-188 expansion and outlasts 133 bequest/129 settlement. No geometry modified.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Modern Greek transcription of an attested Hellenistic mosaic signature, verified through indexed Oxford dissertation page 213 and figure 181; independent museum translation. No visual inspection claimed.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: Courtyard/bathing study has broader third-to-first-century BCE sample. No universal classroom, household toilet, exact household diet or family relationship custom invented. Roman-period Asklepieion treatment accounts and luxury bathing are not backdated.
